title: The Moon is still the same Moon
summary: The same moon can mean reunion, memory, or simply another night. A reflection on how place, experience, and distance shape what each of us sees.
body:
This Mid-Autumn Festival, something occurred to me.

The same day can mean completely different things to different people.

For much of the world, today is simply another Friday. In Korea, it is Chuseok—a time to go home, honor one’s ancestors, and eat songpyeon; many people there may not even know what a mooncake is. In China, it is Mid-Autumn Festival: family, reunion, and mooncakes.

The day is still the same day. The moon is still the same moon.

What changes is the person looking at it.

Over the years, I’ve lived in different countries and cities and done very different kinds of work—from hospitals and laboratories to sales, product, and business leadership; from research and real estate to restaurants and e-commerce. The farther I’ve traveled, the less certain I’ve become that anything is simply “the way it is.”

The smell of coffee on Yonge Street in Toronto on a quiet morning and the scent of pine around Mount Rainier are both wonderful, but they belong to entirely different worlds.

In Barcelona, ten in the morning can feel like the day is only beginning, and dinner at eight or nine is perfectly normal. After years in North America and Asia, even the clock seems to run differently there.

In Sydney, an ordinary bird on the street might be a brightly colored parrot. In Seattle, it’s more likely to be a crow. Live in Korea long enough, and you get used to magpies outside your window.

None of this feels remarkable to the people who live there. To them, that is simply what life looks like.

And that is precisely the point: we have a tendency to mistake the world we see every day for the way the world actually is.

Stay in one place long enough, and it becomes easy to mistake local consensus for universal truth. What counts as success? How much money is enough? What should you have accomplished by a certain age? What is worth holding on to, and what should you let go?

Hear the same answers often enough, and you begin to think that this is simply how life is supposed to be.

I’ve come to believe that our surroundings shape us far more deeply than we realize. They don’t just determine whom we meet or what opportunities come our way. Quietly, they also shape what we are capable of imagining.

Sometimes the real boundary in a person’s life isn’t “I can’t do that.”

It’s never having imagined: Wait—life can be like that?

Change your surroundings, and many things you once took for granted become questions again. Something everyone cares about in one place may mean almost nothing somewhere else. A life considered unconventional in one culture may be perfectly ordinary in another.

I notice this at work, too.

A room full of people can spend hours arguing over A versus B. These days, I’m more inclined to ask: Why does it have to be A or B?

Eventually, I started questioning the question itself.

Who decided this was the problem? Why are we trying to solve it? What if we’re answering the wrong question altogether?

Maybe that’s also why I enjoy arguing less than I used to.

When I was younger, I thought that if you explained something clearly enough, people would understand.

I don’t believe that anymore.

We never communicate through words alone. Behind every sentence stands the life of the person saying it.

Where you grew up. How your parents loved you. What you read. What work you did. Where you traveled. Whom you met. What you gained. What you lost.

All of it becomes part of how you understand even a single sentence.

So two people can speak the same language and use the same words, yet not really be talking about the same thing at all.

Once I understood that, a lot of arguments stopped feeling worth having.

Not because I think I’m right.

Quite the opposite. I’m increasingly aware that what I see is only one angle.

So much of life is perception.

And perhaps that is why I’ve come to value something much rarer.

Every now and then, you meet someone who knows where you’re going before you finish the sentence.

Not because they agree with you.

But because, for a moment, you realize:

Oh. You’ve been here too.

That, to me, is what being “on the same wavelength” really means. It doesn’t mean two people are alike in every way, and it certainly doesn’t require some grand idea of soulmates. It simply means that two people have traveled very different roads and somehow arrived at a few of the same places—places where explanation is no longer necessary.

That kind of understanding is rare.

Familiarity, on the other hand, has its own inertia.

People who have known you for years naturally understand the person you are today through the person you used to be. They may not be wrong. But stay too long inside familiar expectations, and sometimes, without realizing it, you begin living along the lines of your own past.

That is why leaving familiar places once in a while can be a good thing.

Not because you are running away.

But because somewhere new, no one knows who you used to be. No one has already decided who you are supposed to become. Things you stopped questioning long ago suddenly become questions again:

Why does it have to be this way?

Maybe that is also why, as I get older, there are a few things I find increasingly difficult to compromise on: beauty, depth of thought, and love.

They may seem unrelated, but perhaps they share something.

Once you have truly seen certain things, it becomes difficult to pretend you haven’t.

Once you have seen something genuinely beautiful, the ordinary is still ordinary, but you can no longer confuse the two. Once you have thought deeply about a question, a shallow answer rarely satisfies you again.

Perhaps much of life works this way.

The world you have seen eventually becomes part of who you are.

So I’ve also become more comfortable with the fact that some people will never fully understand me, and I will never fully understand them.

That’s all right.

No two people have walked exactly the same road. Why should we expect them to see everything the same way?

Stay curious. Don’t be too quick to dismiss something simply because you haven’t encountered it before. And just because you have traveled a few more roads, don’t assume you are standing any higher than anyone else.

The world is enormous. Each of us sees only a small piece of it.

As for understanding, perhaps it was never something that could be explained into existence.

And somehow, that brings me back to the moon.

Some people are celebrating Chuseok. Some are celebrating Mid-Autumn Festival. Some have no idea that today is anything special at all.

Some are gathered with family. Some are on the road. Some are thinking of home. And some are thinking of someone they haven’t seen in a very long time.

We meet many people over the course of a life. Some stay with us for years; others walk beside us only for a while. Where they eventually go, how their lives turn out—we may never know. The world is wide, and some people, once our paths part, we may truly never see again.

I used to think that seeing someone meant crossing the distance between you and standing face to face.

Now I’m not so sure.

As long as we are still somewhere in this world, we are living through the same stretch of time. We may look up at the same moon, feel the wind of the same season, and quietly go on living our separate lives without knowing anything about each other.

Perhaps remembering someone once in a while is its own kind of meeting.

And if you let the thought travel a little farther, it becomes even more remarkable.

Hundreds of years ago, thousands of years ago, people looked up at this same moon.

They spoke languages different from ours and lived lives we can barely imagine. They are long gone now, but longing itself does not seem to have changed very much.

Generation after generation has entrusted the same moon with thoughts of reunion, home, separation, and the people they missed. Thousands of years of human joy and sorrow, all looking in the same direction.

Seen that way, perhaps it is a good thing that the universe is so vast.

There are so many words left unsaid, so many people we never saw again, so much longing carried across oceans, mountains, and years.

All of it needs somewhere large enough to exist.

The moon, of course, knows none of this.

It knows nothing of Mid-Autumn Festival or Chuseok. It doesn’t know who is together tonight and who is missing someone.

Joy and sorrow, home and separation—those belong to us.

For thousands of years, the moon has simply risen as it always has, shining on the roads that brought us here and on the people who eventually went their separate ways.

And each of us looks up at it carrying an entire lifetime of our own.

The moon is still the same moon.

title: It Had Been There All Along
summary: A fallen leaf, a childhood promise, and the memory of a grandmother become a meditation on presence, absence, and learning to notice what was there all along.
body:
On the same day in late September, I found myself at Incheon Airport again.

Last time, I was here to see off an old friend I had reunited with after many years.

This time, I was the one leaving.

On my way to work this morning, I noticed that the first leaves had already begun to fall.

There was nothing remarkable about the one at my feet. I didn’t even know which tree it had fallen from.

I had walked past that spot every day all summer. Seoul summers can be relentless, and perhaps on some morning or afternoon, that leaf had shielded me from the sun for a fleeting moment. In a way, it had been there with me all summer.

Yet I had never once looked up at it.

Only now, in early autumn, after it had let go of the branch and fallen at my feet, did I really see it for the first time.

Perhaps we are all like that.

Some things are there for so long that they simply become part of the background of our lives. Only when their place is suddenly empty do we realize how much space they once occupied within us.

When I was a child, my grandmother adored me.

Every Saturday night, I would be too excited to sleep because the next morning I got to go to her house and be the little boy who could get away with absolutely anything.

Once, I casually mentioned that the other kids all had jianzi—the little feathered shuttlecocks we kicked around as children.

I forgot about it almost immediately.

She didn’t.

When I was nine, my grandmother, who lived alone, passed away suddenly.

When she died, she was still holding an unfinished jianzi in her hand.

The moment I saw it, I remembered what I had said.

A passing remark from a child had somehow become an assignment I had unknowingly left for her.

She never got to finish it.

I shook her hand and called out to her, over and over, but she no longer answered.

Later, one of the adults handed me a small shovel and told me that the ashes in front of me were my grandmother.

That was the first time I understood what it really meant when someone was “gone.”

It didn’t mean they weren’t here today.

It didn’t mean they would come back in a few days.

It meant they would never come back.

Decades have passed, but I still remember that moment with extraordinary clarity. And even now, I often dream of her.

In my dreams, she is exactly as she used to be, as though she had never left.

I ask her, “If you’ve been here all along, why haven’t you come to see me?

Why have you been hiding from me?”

She never answers.

She simply looks at me quietly, her eyes full of love.

And then I wake up.

In the darkened room, there is only silence—

and a pillow wet with tears.

This summer, while traveling through Hokkaido, I walked into a little shop in Otaru and saw four Japanese characters on the door:

Ichigo ichie.

“One time, one meeting.”

I had known the phrase for years. But that day, for some reason, it suddenly became real.

I remember thinking that I would probably never walk into that little shop again.

Even if I returned to Otaru many years from now, the street might still be there, the doorway might still be there, but the person who greeted me so warmly that day probably wouldn’t be.

And even if they were, I would no longer be the person I was that day.

Places can be revisited.

Time cannot.

Along the way, I passed places that felt strangely familiar: railway tracks beside the sea, the ocean appearing at the end of a sloping street, a quiet corner I somehow felt I had seen before.

Then I remembered.

I had seen them in animation.

Long before I arrived, perhaps an artist had once stood in that same place, in another season and another kind of light, and captured one fleeting moment of what was before them.

Years later, I arrived there from an entirely different life.

We had never met. We hadn’t even existed in that place at the same moment.

And yet, our eyes had rested on the same sea, the same street.

As if we had missed each other in time, only to meet again in another dimension.

When you think about it, the odds of two people ever meeting are astonishingly small.

First, you have to be alive in the same era.

Then you have to find yourselves in the same city.

And even then, you have to pass through the same place at the same time.

If you somehow start talking, share a meal, laugh together, become friends, and end up occupying even a small chapter of each other’s lives—

that already feels a little like winning the lottery.

The strange thing is, when we win, we usually don’t know it.

While working in Korea, I often told my colleagues that performance matters. KPIs matter. Numbers matter.

But a month from now, a year from now, you probably won’t remember most of them.

What you will remember are the people.

You will remember who helped you when you were exhausted. Who hurt you. Who truly listened when you needed to be heard. And you will remember how you treated one another.

Those things can stay with us for years.

So I often tell my team: come to work with some joy.

Because one day, we will all go our separate ways.

Someone will change teams. Someone will change companies. Someone will move to another country.

The person sitting beside you today—the one you meet with, have lunch with, complain and laugh with—may, a few years from now, become someone you can barely find an opportunity to see.

Org charts will change.

Today’s numbers will be replaced by tomorrow’s.

But in this enormous world, somehow, for a few years, we happened to walk into the same building every morning.

That, too, is ichigo ichie.

The airport announcement sounds again.

Some people are arriving. Some are leaving. Some are waving goodbye. Others are pulling their suitcases toward the gate.

Last time I stood here, I watched someone leave.

This time, it is my turn.

We rarely know which time will be the last time.

The last time you have dinner together, the food is still warm.

The last time you say goodbye, you probably just say, “See you next time.”

No one taps you on the shoulder and tells you:

This is the final scene the two of you will ever share.

So if there is no next time, that doesn’t make what came before any less real.

Celebrate every friendship.

Celebrate the roads you walked together, the meals you shared, the ridiculous conversations that meant nothing and somehow meant everything.

Celebrate the people whose lives, for one brief moment in the vastness of time and space, happened to overlap with yours.

Not every journey has to last until the end for the meeting to have been worthwhile.

Before boarding, I thought again about the fallen leaf I had seen that morning.

All summer long, I had never once looked up at it.

Only after it fell did I finally stop and really see it.

It had been there all along.

title: What the World Cannot Take Away
summary: Twenty-five years after September 11, a story of Gander, Paris, grief, and music asks what loss can change—and what it can never take away.
body:
Two things happened this week that, at first, seemed completely unrelated.

September 11 marked twenty-five years since 9/11.

And in Paris, Céline Dion walked back onto a concert stage.

Thirty thousand people had come to see a woman who had not completed a full concert in six years. When the music began, she was already in tears during the first song.

Then came “All By Myself.”

Everyone knew the note that was coming.

She hit it.

When it was over, she let out a long breath and turned toward her band, with a look that seemed to say:

I can’t believe I can still do this.

The entire arena rose to its feet.

Later, she told the crowd simply:

“Je vais bien.”

I’m doing fine.

And somehow, those three words brought thirty thousand people to tears.

Watching her, I suddenly thought of another group of people in the sky twenty-five years ago.

On September 11, 2001, I was in medical school.

I watched New York on television—the planes hitting the towers, smoke swallowing the streets. I was shocked. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing.

But years later, I would look back with some shame at how much of a spectator I had been.

I didn’t yet understand that the day would change the world.

After living in America for many years, I came to understand something else: behind every number in a tragedy is an entire human life—a parent, a spouse, a child, and a chair at the dinner table that will remain empty.

When we are young, suffering seems far away.

Eventually we learn that none of us really stands outside it.

Most of us remember the planes that struck America.

But I wonder how many people have ever asked:

What happened to all the other planes in the sky that day?

When the United States abruptly closed its airspace, flights already crossing the Atlantic suddenly had nowhere to go.

Canada launched Operation Yellow Ribbon, taking in more than 200 aircraft and over 30,000 stranded travelers.

Thirty-eight of those planes landed in Gander, Newfoundland.

Gander had a population of roughly 10,000.

And suddenly, 6,700 strangers fell out of the sky.

There were babies on those planes.

So people on the ground went to drugstores, bought formula and diapers, and brought them out to aircraft whose doors could not yet be opened.

The people of Gander were afraid too.

What if there were terrorists among these strangers?

They opened their doors anyway.

Schools closed and became shelters. Churches and community centers filled with mattresses. Even striking bus drivers returned to work, because thousands of people needed rides.

People ran out of medication; local pharmacies filled their prescriptions. Some passengers had not showered in days; families took complete strangers home.

The whole town started cooking.

There was so much food that the community ice rink became a giant refrigerator.

A town of ten thousand had suddenly grown by more than half.

And afterward, locals spoke about it as though they had done nothing remarkable.

Someone needed help.

So they helped.

Those few days eventually inspired the musical Come From Away.

But the story didn’t end when the planes left.

On one flight home, a passenger asked a simple question:

These people fed us, housed us, opened their homes to us—and refused to take our money.

What can we leave behind?

Someone had an idea:

Let’s help send their children to college.

A sheet of paper began making its way through the cabin.

Before the plane even landed, passengers had pledged $15,000. It became a scholarship fund that would help generations of local students continue their education.

Strangers had given them a home for a few days.

They gave the town’s children a piece of their future.

Years later, nearby Appleton received an extraordinary gift: a piece of steel from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

Steel left behind by one of humanity’s darkest acts traveled thousands of miles—not to commemorate hatred, but the kindness of strangers.

Some people had shown the world how cruel human beings could be.

On that very same day, others answered with a bed, a meal, a diaper, an open door:

This is how kind human beings can be.

I first discovered Céline Dion when I was in medical school.

Back then, I simply thought “My Heart Will Go On” was a beautiful song.

Later, I learned about the girl from Quebec, the youngest of fourteen children in a family of modest means, who somehow sang her way into an extraordinary life.

Then her husband, René, developed cancer.

At the height of her career, she stepped back to care for him. After he died in 2016, she eventually returned to the stage.

I saw her perform in Las Vegas during those years. She was standing so close to me.

Some singers, after enough years, stop being merely singers.

Their voices begin to carry pieces of your own youth.

Then Céline became seriously ill.

Stiff-person syndrome.

For a singer, there was something almost unbearably cruel about it. The disease can cause severe muscle rigidity and spasms and can interfere with the physical control required to sing.

A woman whose voice had changed her life was struck by an illness that threatened to take that very voice away.

She disappeared from full concerts for six years.

Many assumed she would never return.

But she kept working.

She retrained her body. Her breathing. Her voice.

Day after day.

Until this September, when she walked back onto a stage in Paris.

Twenty-five songs.

More than two hours.

And the woman who had once faced the possibility of losing her voice sang “My Heart Will Go On” again.

Twenty-five years ago, when I first heard that song, I thought it was about love.

Now I hear something else.

It is also about what happens after loss—when people leave, when things are taken from us, when life can never return to what it was.

And yet, somehow, the heart goes on.

I became Canadian, and later American.

So Canada and the United States have never been simply two neighboring countries on a map to me. Both became home. My feelings for both come from having lived a life in each.

Last September, I experienced reunion and separation.

This September brought a final goodbye.

And still, I choose to believe in certain things.

Because I have seen a small town open its doors when strangers had nowhere else to go.

And I have seen a woman who nearly lost her voice walk back onto a stage six years later and sing the note everyone thought she might never sing again.

We grow old.

People leave.

Many things we once believed we could never lose, we eventually do.

Perhaps what is most precious about being human is not what we manage to hold on to.

It is knowing how fragile life is, and still offering a stranger a bed.

Having so much taken from us, and still finding another song to sing.

Being hurt, and still refusing to lose our capacity to love.

Twenty-five years ago, Gander opened a door.

Twenty-five years later, a light came on in Paris.

We have been hurt, and still choose kindness.
We have lost, and still choose love.
We know how every story ends, and still choose to keep moving forward.

Maybe that is what it has meant all along:

My Heart Will Go On.

title: A Song Beneath Independence Gate
summary: At Seodaemun Independence Park on Korea’s Liberation Day, history, sacrifice, national memory, and one familiar song meet beneath Independence Gate.
body:
Today is August 15, Korea’s National Liberation Day.

During the day in Gwanghwamun, a procession stretched for miles. Korean and American flags waved side by side. Koreans remember that their liberation in 1945 came with America’s defeat of Japan. They also remember that, in the war that followed only a few years later, the United States helped defend the country and the democracy it would become.

That evening, I happened to pass Seodaemun Independence Park and came across the Seodaemun Independence & Democracy Festival.

The stage stood beside Seodaemun Prison History Hall. Many Korean independence activists were once imprisoned here. Some never walked out.

Behind the stage stood Dongnimmun—Independence Gate.

Built in 1897, it commemorated Korea’s emergence from Qing China’s influence and its aspiration to stand as an independent nation. Yet only a few years later, Korea began losing its sovereignty. From 1905 to 1945, that struggle lasted forty years; formal Japanese colonial rule lasted thirty-five.

For a small country caught between great powers, there must have been many moments when hope seemed almost impossible. Yet its people never gave up their language, their culture, or their traditions.

After living here for more than a year and getting to know the country up close, I sometimes find Koreans stubborn, blunt, and unwilling to bend. At other times, I find myself deeply moved by that same intensity—their warmth, solidarity, and sheer determination to hold on.

I turned on Google Translate to follow one of the speeches from the stage. The message, roughly, was this: the country would continue to care for the families of those who had sacrificed for it.

Not simply as a political gesture, but so that generation after generation could believe in something fundamental:

If you love and protect your country, your country will protect you, too.

For the independence and continuity of a nation, that belief matters enormously.

It reminded me of something a Korean colleague once told me about the 1997 Asian financial crisis. Ordinary Koreans brought out their gold jewelry and donated it to help the country repay its foreign debt. Her father even had a gold tooth removed from his mouth and donated that.

When a country is in trouble, its people hold it up.

And a country, in turn, must never forget those who once held it up.

Later that evening, Lena Park (박정현) came onstage to sing.

Of all the songs performed that night, there was only one whose every word I understood.

By coincidence—or perhaps fittingly—it was “You Raise Me Up.”

title: The Way Life Should Be
summary: A road trip through Osoyoos and Penticton reveals roadside honesty stands, volunteer firefighters, and the quiet trust that makes a place worth remembering.
body:
After returning from Seoul, I took a road trip through Osoyoos and Penticton.

Most of my memories of British Columbia are of the coast around Vancouver—the ocean, the forests, and that deep green that seems to stay wet year-round. But heading east this time, I discovered an entirely different landscape.

The mountains grew drier and more rugged, with sparse vegetation and sharply defined ridgelines. Through the valleys and along the highways stretched endless apple orchards, vineyards, and wineries, with one lake appearing after another.

It reminded me a lot of Lake Chelan and Wenatchee in Washington—the same valleys, the same orchards, the same little towns that seem to have grown up around the water.

Only there were far fewer people.

Sometimes I could drive along a lake for an hour and barely see another person. That sense of emptiness reminded me of northern Ontario.

Coming back from Gangnam in Seoul made the contrast even more striking.

Just days earlier, I had been surrounded by packed subway cars, work, meetings, numbers, messages—everything pushing you to move faster. Then suddenly I was here, as if someone had pressed the slow-motion button on life.

Cars moved slowly. People walked slowly. Boats drifted slowly. Wine was sipped slowly.

At first, it almost felt strange.

Before I moved to Asia, I used to vacation at Lake Chelan every year. On the way there, I would always pass a little farm by the highway.

The farmer would put freshly picked yellow apricots into boxes and leave them on a table by the road. A small sign said: $5 a box.

No cashier. No cameras. No one watching.

Just a little jar for the money.

You took what you wanted and left the cash yourself.

Every time I stopped, there was already plenty of money in the jar.

Once, curiosity got the better of me. Where was the farmer?

I wandered around the side of the property and eventually spotted the family behind the house, floating on the Columbia River.

They were sitting in inner tubes, drinking, laughing, enjoying the afternoon.

Meanwhile, cars kept pulling over by the highway. Strangers picked up fruit, left their money, and drove away.

The family hardly seemed to care.

It was as though the possibility that someone might take the fruit without paying had never even crossed their minds.

This time, in Penticton, after riding an old steam train preserved from the last century, I passed another roadside fruit farm on my way back to our place by the lake.

Again, nobody was there.

The farm was full of apples, grapes, vegetables, and other produce. On a table sat a scale and a price list.

The instructions were obvious:

Pick what you want.
Weigh it yourself.
Work out the price.
Leave the money.

Unfortunately, all I had were a few U.S. dollars and credit cards—no Canadian cash. I stood there looking at the fruit for a while before reluctantly leaving empty-handed.

I was disappointed, but somehow also warmed by the whole thing.

On opposite sides of an international border, these farmers in the valleys of Washington and British Columbia seemed to share the same kind of ease.

It isn’t that they don’t know some people will take advantage of others.

They simply choose to believe that most people won’t.

And perhaps that kind of trust can survive only because most people who pass through are willing to live up to it.

Trust isn’t one person’s naivety. It’s a way of life that a community quietly agrees to protect.

There was another small moment on the road that stayed with me.

We stopped to charge the car in the little town of Entiat. While waiting, I walked into a nearby convenience store and noticed a flyer on the wall recruiting volunteer firefighters.

Wildfires have become a fact of life across the West. People here know better than anyone how quickly a fire can spread—and what it means to run toward one.

There is little pay, sometimes none at all. Yet volunteers still face flames, smoke, and very real danger.

At the bottom of the flyer was a row of tear-off tabs with a phone number.

Many of them were already gone.

I stood there looking at it for a while.

I wondered who had taken them.

Maybe a young man from one of the nearby orchards. Maybe a mechanic. Maybe just some ordinary person in shorts and flip-flops who had passed me a few minutes earlier while buying coffee.

Most days, everyone simply goes about their own lives.

But when the mountains catch fire, someone still has to walk toward the flames.

Standing there, I suddenly felt that the people here somehow belonged to this landscape.

The water is clear.
The fruit is sweet.
The wine is rich.

But strangely, those aren’t the things I remember most.

I remember the unattended jar of money beside the highway.

I remember the farmer and his family floating on the river, drinking and laughing, apparently too busy enjoying life to worry about their roadside stand.

And I remember those little phone-number tabs on the convenience-store wall, already torn away one by one.

After living in Seoul for so long, I had grown accustomed to efficiency, competition, and the feeling that there was always one more thing to get done.

Coming here reminded me that life doesn’t always have to be a race forward.

We can move a little more slowly.

We can trust strangers a little more.

And when someone needs us, we can still be willing to do something for the place we call home.

There is something reciprocal about trust: when you choose to believe in people, they often learn to become worthy of that belief.

The beauty of the mountains and rivers is given by nature.
But what makes a place truly good is something its people build—and protect—a little at a time.

Maybe this is what life is supposed to look like.

title: A Loophole in Natural Selection
summary: One garden walk, four suspicious berries, and a dog-wash faucet become a very funny investigation into curiosity, poison, and natural selection’s quality control.
body:
I was wandering through a garden today when I spotted a fairly tall tree covered in clusters of little black berries.

Shiny, almost black. They looked a lot like the blackcurrants I used to eat as a kid.

Only problem: they were a little too high up.

I stood under the tree staring at them for a while, getting hungrier by the second. Eventually I went up on my toes, stretched as far as I could, and after some serious effort managed to pull one down.

Bit into it.

Jesus. So bitter.

Only then did it occur to me:

What the hell is this thing?

So I took a picture and asked AI.

Cherry laurel. The pits and leaves contain cyanogenic compounds that can release hydrogen cyanide when crushed or chewed. Do not eat.

…

Cyanide.

Why does that word sound so familiar?

Oh, right. Isn’t that the stuff spies in old espionage novels keep around for when they get captured?

I looked down at my phone. Then back up at the tree.

Suddenly, the image of myself standing on tiptoe, straining to reach that berry, seemed oddly inspirational.

Some dangers don’t come looking for you. You have to stand on your toes and work for them.

I spat it out immediately, although that indescribable bitterness followed me down the path.

A little farther on, I found another tree covered in bright red berries.

Glossy. Plump. Hanging in cheerful little clusters.

These looked much more trustworthy.

Picked one.

Tasted it.

Took a picture.

Asked AI.

Holly.

The berries contain saponins and other compounds. Eating enough can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

…

Fine.

Kept walking.

Then I spotted another little red fruit tucked among some needle-like leaves. It looked like a tiny red lantern.

Absolutely beautiful.

By now, I had experience.

So this time I only ate one.

Red, soft, and—surprisingly—a little sweet.

As usual, after eating it, I took a picture and asked AI.

This time AI opened with:

“STOP. This one is more dangerous.”

Yew.

And this plant is particularly devious. The soft red flesh on the outside has relatively low toxicity—it’s basically there to tempt birds into eating it and spreading the seeds.

The real trouble is inside. The seed and other parts of the plant contain taxine alkaloids. If the seed is chewed, the toxins can affect the heart and, in severe cases, can be fatal.

Why are birds okay?

Because apparently birds are smarter than I am.

They swallow the seeds whole.

I, on the other hand, picked one myself and thoughtfully sampled it like I was judging a wine competition.

The first two berries were mainly exploring the question of how quickly I could get to a bathroom.

This one had moved on to how my estate should be divided.

At this point, I realized the relationship between this tree and me was no longer one between a plant and a visitor.

It was fishing.

And I had taken the bait. 😂

Now, any adult of normal intelligence would have concluded the day’s wild-berry tasting session right there.

I did not.

Because a little later, I found some white berries.

Round. Plump. Almost translucent.

They had the innocent face of something that had never done anything wrong in its life.

So I conducted a highly rigorous scientific analysis in my head:

Black ones are poisonous.

Red ones are poisonous.

Surely the white ones can’t be poisonous too?

Pick.

Taste.

Photograph.

AI:

“Are you deliberately trying to eat every poisonous ornamental berry you can find today? That’s snowberry. It contains saponins and can cause vomiting. You’ve basically sampled everything. Do you need me to call 911?”

…

At this point, I actually got a little annoyed.

If none of you are meant to be eaten, WHY DO YOU ALL INSIST ON LOOKING LIKE FRUIT?

One afternoon:

Cherry laurel. Holly. Yew. Snowberry.

Cyanogenic compounds. Saponins. Taxines…

Other people go to a garden to enjoy the flowers and scenery.

I went for one walk and reviewed botany, toxicology, and clinical medicine.

And my research methodology was cutting-edge:

Phase I human trial first. Literature review afterward.

Eventually, the more I read, the more nervous I got, so I decided I should probably rinse my mouth out.

Small problem.

Where do you find drinking water in the middle of a garden?

I searched for ages until I finally spotted a row of faucets.

Ran over.

The sign above them said:

DOG WASH.

I stood there for about two seconds, reconsidering several of my life choices.

Whatever.

Life before dignity.

So a few people out walking their dogs got to watch a visibly not-very-bright middle-aged man crouching beside the dog-washing station, vigorously rinsing his mouth.

One dog stared at me the entire time.

I understood the look perfectly:

“Dude… you eat shit too?”

On the way home, something finally occurred to me.

A genuinely serious question.

Why didn’t I take the picture and ask AI before I ate the fruit?

My phone was literally in my hand.

Was I really that hungry?

I couldn’t wait ten seconds?

Even more disturbing, I repeated the exact same sequence four times today:

See fruit.

Eat fruit.

Take picture.

Discover it’s poisonous.

Keep walking.

See another one.

Eat again.

I’ve been alive for quite a few years now, but today was the first time I seriously wondered:

Given my level of curiosity—and this particular order of operations—

how the hell have I survived this long?

After giving it some thought, there’s really only one possible conclusion:

Natural selection clearly has some quality-control issues. 😂

title: Seoul, This Summer Is Almost Well Done
summary: I opened my weather app this morning. 35°C. Feels like 38°C. At this point, I’m convinced that if the morning sun shines on me for more than thirty seconds, I’ll turn into medium-rare Wagyu.
body:
I opened my weather app this morning.

35°C.

Feels like 38°C.

At this point, I’m convinced that if the morning sun shines on me for more than thirty seconds, I’ll turn into medium-rare Wagyu.

I came across an interesting news story recently. Korea has always eaten bluefin tuna, but most of it arrived frozen, while the freshest catch usually went straight to Japan.

This year is different.

As the ocean warms, giant bluefin tuna—some over two meters long and weighing more than 100 kilograms—are becoming increasingly common in Korea’s East Sea.

The fish no longer has to cross an ocean. It can be swimming in the morning, sitting on a shelf at Lotte Mart by the afternoon, and served at someone's dinner table that evening.

Working in eCommerce, my first thought wasn't climate change.

It was the supply chain.

The shipping distance disappeared.

Cold-chain costs disappeared.

Several layers of the supply chain disappeared.

Who would have thought that the thing solving part of the supply-chain problem wouldn't be logistics?

Or AI.

It would be climate.

For years we've talked about climate change—reducing emissions, protecting the environment, driving less. The usual response is always the same:

"Yeah... we should really do something about it."

Eventually.

But put a box of fresher—and cheaper—bluefin tuna in front of people, and suddenly opinions evolve remarkably fast.

I found myself feeling a little jealous of the tuna.

At least it gets to stay fresh.

By the time I walk from my apartment to the subway station, I'm already half cooked.

This morning I rushed out the door and tossed half a chocolate bar into my pocket, thinking I'd eat it on the train.

When I reached into my pocket for my phone...

I pulled out my phone—and a handful of melted chocolate.

😑

For a few seconds, my brain simply stopped working.

No tissues.

No water.

Nine subway stops to go.

There was no way I was going to spend the rest of the ride holding one sticky hand in the air.

So I made what I believed was the most rational decision an adult could make.

The most environmentally friendly solution available.

The Korean passenger sitting across from me watched my expression go from confusion...

to horror...

to quiet determination...

before slowly sliding a little farther away.

I can only imagine what was going through his mind.

"What exactly... did that foreigner just pull out of his pocket?" 🤢

Only later did I realize...

the thing that had really melted wasn't the chocolate.

It was my social reputation in Korea.

So this week, I told my team to work from home.

Not because it would make us more productive.

Simply because making it to the office without melting into liquid already feels like an achievement.

Even those few minutes between the subway station and the office leave me feeling like I'm being slow-cooked into an immortality pill.

Dear God...

would You mind turning the sun down just a little?

Summer has arrived.

It's time for Your air-conditioning miracle.

Then again, maybe whenever God closes a door and a window...

it's because He's turning on the AC.

I'll stop here.

Any hotter,

and this weather is officially becoming rude.

title: A Thousand Booths, A Thousand Interesting Souls
summary: Today I visited the Seoul Illustration Fair for the first time. I thought it was just another design market. I couldn't have been more wrong. Inside were nearly a thousand independent artists.
body:
Today I visited the Seoul Illustration Fair for the first time.

I thought it was just another design market.

I couldn't have been more wrong.

Inside were nearly a thousand independent artists.

Each one quietly creating a world of their own.

Some drew foxes, rabbits, and cats, turning them into plush toys, keychains, and stickers.

Others transformed their original characters into umbrellas, T-shirts, mugs, and home décor.

Some simply sat there sketching while inviting visitors to create alongside them.

I waited twenty minutes just to get in.

The place was packed all day.

Then something suddenly clicked.

I finally understood why Korea feels so effortlessly charming.

The tiny icons in the subway.

The illustrations on buses.

Convenience-store packaging.

Coffee shop menus.

Street posters.

Even public signs somehow make you smile.

It's not because a handful of brilliant designers created everything.

It's because thousands of people are creating, every single day.

Most of their work will never become a bestseller.

But together, they keep feeding the city new ideas.

I love that kind of creative ecosystem.

It feels like a place where people are encouraged to make what they genuinely love.

Some people will love it.

Others won't.

That's okay.

Make it anyway.

There were plenty of hands-on workshops too, where visitors could sit down and create something of their own.

I painted two tiny surfboards.

They looked like something a kindergartener would proudly bring home. 😂

Oddly enough, I wasn't embarrassed in the slightest.

The best thing I took home today wasn't something I bought.

It was a realization.

A city's creativity isn't built by a few extraordinary geniuses.

It's built by thousands of ordinary people who are willing to turn a small idea in their heads into something someone else wants to take home.

Enough of those little ideas, given enough time, become a culture.

Maybe that's why, walking around Korea, even cuteness feels like it has an entire ecosystem behind it.

Some kinds of joy don't translate very well.

But sometimes...

all it takes is one walk around the room to understand them.

title: Team Building Was Never About the Dinner
summary: Last week, I took my team on a dinner cruise along the Han River. Every quarter, I choose a few teammates to receive a small gift. This July, it was a U.S. Marine Corps pin.
body:
Last week, I took my team on a dinner cruise along the Han River.

Every quarter, I choose a few teammates to receive a small gift.

This July, it was a U.S. Marine Corps pin.

The Marines have a simple motto:

Semper Fidelis. Always Faithful.

Every Marine knows they can trust the person beside them with their life—and they know they are expected to be that person for someone else.

A company isn't a battlefield, of course.

But I've always believed that great teams are built on the same kind of trust.

When something goes wrong, no one should have to ask for help. Someone simply steps forward.

That's why I never give this pin to the highest performer.

I give it to the people who make everyone else feel more confident doing their job.

There was another surprise that evening.

It turned out one of our teammates was a magician.

Halfway through dinner, he casually started performing card tricks at the table, leaving everyone laughing and trying to figure out how he'd done them.

It reminded me that this is what makes a team interesting.

Some people solve impossible problems.

Some create unforgettable moments.

Some lead from the front.

Others quietly make sure no one falls behind.

Everyone contributes differently.

And that's exactly why a team becomes stronger.

Thank you to everyone who makes our team a little better every day.

title: At Gyeongpo Lake, I Didn't Spend Much Time Looking at the Lake
summary: If someone asked me what the most beautiful thing about Gyeongpo Lake was, I probably wouldn't say the lake. The lake itself is beautiful, of course. I stayed on the top floor of Skybay Hotel. From my room, the East...
body:
If someone asked me what the most beautiful thing about Gyeongpo Lake was,

I probably wouldn't say the lake.

The lake itself is beautiful, of course.

I stayed on the top floor of Skybay Hotel. From my room, the East Sea stretched out on one side, Gyeongpo Lake on the other. Open the window and both the sea breeze and the lake breeze drifted in together. In the morning, the water was so still it looked like polished glass. By evening, clouds slowly settled across the sky while lotus leaves swayed gently and an occasional heron skimmed the surface.

It was all beautiful.

But the thing that kept making me stop wasn't the landscape.

It was a series of tiny bronze sculptures scattered around the lake.

Most of them were only thirty or forty centimeters tall.

At first, I took a photo almost absentmindedly.

Then I noticed another sculpture a few meters later.

And another.

And another.

Together, they quietly told hundreds of little stories.

Two young people meeting for the first time. A nervous boy unsure where to put his hands. A young man pretending to be calm while secretly checking whether the girl smiled after receiving his flowers. Lovers falling in love. Lovers saying goodbye. One chasing. One waiting. One quietly crying while the other pretended everything was fine.

Farther along the path stood a young swordsman, a rider on horseback, an old fortune teller counting on his fingers, a child desperately trying to outrun a puppy, naked children laughing together, and a little girl whose tears had been carved permanently onto her face.

None of the sculptures were large.

Yet each one managed to preserve a single moment forever.

What fascinated me most were their expressions.

One laughed so hard it looked as though they might fall over.

Another stared in complete disbelief, mouth frozen open.

One cried with tears etched into bronze.

A little boy held a wooden stick high above his head, as if he were about to swing it at any second.

I stood there much longer than I expected.

Eventually, I caught myself smiling back.

They weren't people from my time.

Some were scholars.

Some were generals.

Some were old.

Others were children.

Centuries separated the clothes they wore from the ones I wear today.

Yet laughter still looked like laughter.

Tears still looked like tears.

And falling in love looked exactly the same.

I cycled slowly around the lake, stopping at one sculpture after another.

Without realizing it, I had quietly traveled through centuries of Korean history.

At one point, while photographing another bronze figure, I noticed a girl who looked Russian stop beside the very same sculpture.

She lifted her phone and spent several minutes taking pictures.

Neither of us said a word.

We simply smiled, nodded to each other, and continued on our separate ways.

Maybe curiosity doesn't need translation.

After completing the entire loop, I went back to my hotel and scrolled through the photos I'd taken.

Only then did I realize something.

The subject I had photographed most wasn't Gyeongpo Lake.

It wasn't the lotus flowers.

It wasn't even the East Sea.

It was the people who never moved.

Later that afternoon, I reached the far side of the lake and found an enormous moon sculpture.

I stood there, very seriously pretending to push it.

Needless to say...

it didn't move.

Long after leaving Gangneung, I still find myself thinking about Gyeongpo Lake.

But strangely,

I don't think about the lake first.

I think about those tiny bronze figures.

In the last photograph I took,

every one of them was still exactly where they'd always been.

There was only one difference.

Now there was one more person beside the lake—

trying to push the moon.

title: Today, My Liver Had Layers
summary: Last Sunday, I stopped by the Seoul Bar & Spirits Show. Five minutes after walking in, I realized something: Everyone in Seoul who truly loves a drink had somehow gathered in the same place.
body:
Last Sunday, I stopped by the Seoul Bar & Spirits Show.

Five minutes after walking in, I realized something:

Everyone in Seoul who truly loves a drink had somehow gathered in the same place.

More than a hundred booths offered a passport-free tour of the world's spirits.

Moutai. Johnnie Walker. Tequila. Gin. Vodka. Japanese whisky...

Every few steps, someone would hand me another tiny tasting glass.

The most dangerous sentence of the day?

"Just one sip."

Because every booth said exactly the same thing.

A few dozen "just one sips" later, an entire afternoon had quietly disappeared.

Every spirit came with its perfect companion—orange slices, dark chocolate, lime wedges, smoked sausage, cheese...

I used to think they were simply snacks.

Then I realized their real job was to defend every glass:

"It's not harsh—it's layered."

"It's not burning—it's the finish."

"It's not strong—it's the lingering sweetness."

The staff were wonderfully serious about the ritual.

"Smell it first. Then sip. Notice the opening notes, the middle, and the finish."

I nodded with equal seriousness.

After enough tastings, I began wondering whether the spirits were actually becoming more complex—or if my tongue had simply become increasingly cooperative.

Every brand proudly claimed,

"Our spirits have incredible layers."

By the end of the afternoon, I realized the thing with the most layers wasn't the whisky.

It was my liver.

The top shelf was tequila.

The middle shelf was Scotch.

The basement belonged to Moutai.

None of them seemed to know each other.

After more than two hours of tasting, I was surprisingly sober.

For a moment I wondered if a year of living in Seoul had quietly trained me for this.

Then it hit me.

It wasn't that my alcohol tolerance had improved.

It was that every brand was only responsible for getting you slightly tipsy.

Together, they worked remarkably well as a team.

By the end of the show, the most sober people in Seoul were all trying very hard to convince everyone they weren't drunk.

Myself included.

Although...

On the subway ride home, it did seem as if the train had developed a noticeably better sense of rhythm.

🍸

title: Seongyojang: The Bridge Is Gone, but Home Remains
summary: Most people visit Gangneung for the East Sea. Or the cafés. Or BTS filming locations. Or the beach from Goblin. The place that made me stop, however, was an old estate that many visitors never even hear about.
body:
Most people visit Gangneung for the East Sea.

Or the cafés.

Or BTS filming locations.

Or the beach from Goblin.

The place that made me stop, however, was an old estate that many visitors never even hear about.

It's called Seongyojang.

Three hundred years ago, it wasn't called that at all.

Back then, Gyeongpo Lake stretched much farther inland, reaching almost to the front gate of the estate. There was no road home. Instead, people tied together more than a dozen wooden boats to form a floating bridge, crossing the gently rocking water each day.

Over time, the lake gradually receded.

The boats disappeared.

The bridge disappeared.

Only the name remained—Seongyojang, literally "the estate of the boat bridge"—preserving the memory of a lake that no longer exists.

The owner of the estate was a man named Yi Naebeon.

History has surprisingly little to say about him.

He wasn't a celebrated general.

He didn't leave behind famous writings.

Official records simply note that he built a residence in Gangneung.

Local legend, however, tells a different story.

While searching for land to build his home, Yi supposedly noticed a family of weasels quietly making their way through the woods.

He followed them until they stopped beside Gyeongpo Lake.

The wind settled.

The weasels stopped moving.

Looking across the pine forest, the lake, and the distant mountains, he simply said,

"This is the place."

Whether the story is true hardly matters.

Many old houses survive this way.

History preserves facts.

Stories preserve warmth.

Inside Seongyojang, my favorite place wasn't the grand main hall.

It was a modest little pavilion called Yeolhwadang.

The name simply means "a place for joyful conversation."

Nothing grand.

Nothing philosophical.

The owner didn't build it for politics or scholarship.

He built it so friends could drink tea, play chess, watch the snow fall, and let an ordinary afternoon unfold slowly.

Standing there, I realized the people who lived centuries ago may have understood homes better than we do.

A house isn't simply somewhere that keeps out the wind and rain.

It's somewhere people want to return to.

Over the next three centuries, kingdoms fell.

Japanese occupation came and went.

War arrived.

Gyeongpo Lake continued shrinking.

Yet Seongyojang remained.

Ten generations of the same family have lived beneath the same roofs.

Children were born here.

Elders spent their final days here.

The kitchen fires have never truly gone out.

When I left, the evening sun was sinking over Gyeongpo Lake.

The courtyard was almost silent, save for the wind moving gently through the pine trees.

At that moment, I realized that what truly survives time isn't carved beams or beautiful architecture.

It's ordinary life.

The bridge is gone.

The lake has grown smaller.

The dynasty has long since disappeared.

Yet someone still opens this gate every morning and lives beneath the same roof.

Perhaps that's what makes a house legendary.

Not the amount of history it has witnessed—

but the simple fact that, no matter how much the world changes,

someone still calls it home.

title: 250 Years: The Greatest Achievement Isn't Never Making Mistakes
summary: In Chinese, the number 250 has an unfortunate meaning. It roughly describes someone who's foolish or hopelessly naïve. And yet this year, the United States turned 250 years old.
body:
In Chinese, the number 250 has an unfortunate meaning.

It roughly describes someone who's foolish or hopelessly naïve.

And yet this year, the United States turned 250 years old.

While reading about American history, I came across an extraordinary coincidence.

Three U.S. presidents died on Independence Day.

Even more remarkably, Thomas Jefferson and John Adams—two principal authors of the Declaration of Independence—both died on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the nation was born.

Sometimes history writes better stories than Hollywood.

Over the past 250 years, America has produced extraordinary presidents.

It has also produced deeply controversial ones.

Almost every generation eventually asks the same question:

"Is this president really the best we could do?"

The older I get, however, the more I think a country's greatest strength isn't its ability to always elect exceptional leaders.

It's its ability to survive electing imperfect ones.

The Constitution endures.

Presidents come and go.

A mature system isn't one that guarantees perfect decisions.

It's one designed so that no single individual can determine the destiny of an entire nation—and so that mistakes, inevitable as they are, can still be corrected.

That thought eventually led me to AI.

For more than two centuries, humanity has pursued greater productivity.

Artificial intelligence may be the first technology capable of increasing it by an entirely different order of magnitude.

But if AI ultimately produces nothing more than larger market capitalizations for a handful of companies and greater wealth for an even smaller group of people, then it will simply represent the next stage of capitalism.

I hope for something more ambitious.

I hope the productivity created by AI doesn't end as concentrated wealth.

I hope it becomes shared time.

A four-day workweek.

Maybe even three.

More time for family.

For learning.

For creating.

For traveling.

Or simply for doing nothing at all.

The true purpose of technology shouldn't be making people busier.

It should be giving people the freedom not to be busy all the time.

Two hundred and fifty years ago, people fought for political freedom.

Two hundred and fifty years later, I hope AI can help deliver another kind of freedom—

the freedom to own more of our time.

Because the true measure of a successful society isn't how many trillion-dollar companies it creates.

It's whether ordinary people gain more time to live lives that actually belong to them.

title: Pathology Never Assumed Experts Couldn't Be Wrong
summary: How AI Made Me Understand Pathology All Over Again Today I was chatting with several colleagues from eBay and TikTok about platform governance and trust.
body:
How AI Made Me Understand Pathology All Over Again

Today I was chatting with several colleagues from eBay and TikTok about platform governance and trust.

In marketplace governance, a 3% false positive can wrongly punish thousands of legitimate sellers. A single false negative, on the other hand, may expose consumers to significant harm and erode trust in the platform.

Naturally, the conversation turned to AI.

Can AI solve this?

Can we keep pushing accuracy even higher?

At one point, someone was surprised to learn that I graduated from medical school and had previously worked in pathology, focusing on lymphoma, immunohistochemistry, and molecular diagnostics.

That immediately brought me back to my days in Professor Gao Zifen's pathology department.

When I was young, I never understood why pathologists spent so much time discussing a single case.

Why did the immunohistochemistry panel keep expanding?

Why did experts constantly seek second opinions—and sometimes openly disagree with one another?

Why did nobody ever seem completely certain?

Years later, I think I finally understand.

Pathology never assumed experts couldn't be wrong.

Quite the opposite.

It starts with the assumption that people will disagree, drift in judgment, become overconfident, and sometimes even lead an entire community gradually off course without realizing it.

That's why multidisciplinary consultations, double reading, immunohistochemistry, molecular diagnostics, digital pathology, external quality assessment, and today's increasingly important proficiency testing are all expressions of the same philosophy at different stages of technological progress.

Their purpose has never been to prove that we are right.

Their purpose is to keep a complex system continuously calibrated.

The greatest success of pathology proficiency testing is the mistakes that never happen.

In The Black Swan, Nassim Nicholas Taleb describes the idea of Via Negativa.

We naturally reward achievements that happened.

We rarely reward disasters that never occurred because someone prevented them.

Viewed this way, every issue uncovered through proficiency testing represents a real-world error that was eliminated before it could ever reach a patient.

In a sense, proficiency testing records a kind of counterfactual history—events that never happened, yet mattered immensely.

The most dangerous enemy is rarely ignorance.

It's overconfidence.

Donald Rumsfeld famously divided uncertainty into known knowns, known unknowns, and unknown unknowns.

Many of our greatest risks don't come from problems we already recognize.

They come from the problems we haven't yet realized exist.

In complex systems, the greatest threat is often not making mistakes.

It's becoming increasingly confident while quietly drifting away from the truth.

Knowledge eventually outlives individuals.

Systems become its memory.

Pathologists retire.

Young physicians take their place.

Technology evolves—from digital pathology to spatial transcriptomics to AI.

Yet experience continues to be encoded into the system through feedback and calibration, allowing knowledge to survive far longer than any individual expert.

In that sense, external quality assessment and proficiency testing are forms of collective memory.

Great systems don't depend on extraordinary individuals.

They depend on the continuous accumulation, preservation, and transfer of experience.

The greatest strength of an excellent system isn't that it trusts experts.

It's that it refuses to trust anyone completely—including the experts themselves.

Karl Popper wrote in Conjectures and Refutations:

Science progresses not by proving ourselves right, but by exposing ourselves to being wrong.

Science advances not because we continuously prove ourselves correct, but because we continuously create opportunities to discover where we might be wrong.

Looking back now, I think the greatest invention of proficiency testing was never higher accuracy.

It was turning humility into a system.

Institutionalized humility.

Perhaps we've been asking the wrong questions all along.

For years I kept asking:

How can we reduce false positives?

How can we reduce false negatives?

How can we make AI even more accurate?

Today, I'm no longer convinced those are the first-principles questions.

Complex systems will always encounter new risks and new unknowns.

The real challenge has never been eliminating error.

It's discovering mistakes earlier, correcting them faster, and preventing an entire system from slowly drifting in the wrong direction.

Rather than pursuing perfect prediction, perhaps we should pursue continuous calibration.

Rather than relying on increasingly intelligent models, perhaps we should build increasingly honest feedback mechanisms.

Today, I find myself placing less faith in any single expert, any single team, or even any single AI model.

Instead, I trust systems that continuously invite challenge, expose their own weaknesses, and learn from every correction.

Perhaps the true purpose of a complex system is not to prove that it is right.

It is to create endless opportunities to discover where it may be wrong.

Because the deepest form of safety in any complex system never comes from perfection.

It comes from its ability to continually correct itself.

The greatest danger isn't making mistakes.

It's when an entire community slowly drifts away from reality—and no one notices.

And the most dangerous mistakes are often the ones that make us feel increasingly certain that we're right.

title: My Second Asian Summer in Seoul
summary: My Second Summer in Asia Last summer, I took a vacation in Tokyo. It was so hot I questioned every life decision that had brought me there.
body:
My Second Summer in Asia

Last summer, I took a vacation in Tokyo.

It was so hot I questioned every life decision that had brought me there.

This year, I learned my lesson.

I headed north.

To Hokkaido.

As it turns out, maps don't lie.

The moment I stepped off the plane, it was below 20°C.

I instantly forgave Asia for having summers.

From Sapporo to Furano, Biei, Asahikawa, Otaru, and finally Tomakomai, one thing stayed remarkably consistent.

Everything was...

Clean.

Exceptionally clean.

How clean?

I spent half the trip looking for a trash can.

Eventually I realized that while trash cans weren't always easy to find...

Trash itself was nowhere to be found.

Not along the roads.

Not in the cities.

Nowhere.

Then I noticed something else.

Japanese cars are tiny.

Tiny enough that, from a distance, they look like little cartoon cars patiently commuting to work.

If you parked an American SUV beside them, it would feel like one sneeze could send three kei cars rolling down the street.

Even more surprising?

During the entire road trip, I didn't hear a single car horn.

Not one.

For a while, I honestly wondered whether Japanese cars simply weren't manufactured with horns.

Eventually, when no one was around, I found an empty road and quietly tested the theory.

The horn worked.

People just had incredible patience.

The kind of patience that almost didn't seem human.

At least not by the standards of most American drivers...

or Korean drivers.

Then there was the air.

Public spaces didn't smell like cigarette smoke.

It reminded me of downtown Seattle, where the air often carries a scent that's difficult to identify.

Is it marijuana?

Homelessness?

Or someone who smoked marijuana and then decided to mark their territory the way certain animals do?

Compared to that, Seoul is already doing quite well.

Smoking areas are concentrated.

You still end up inhaling a little of someone else's life every time you walk past one.

Japan solved the problem differently.

Smokers get their own little glass rooms.

Inside, clouds of smoke.

Outside, peaceful streets.

The smokers smoke.

Everyone else keeps walking.

Nobody bothers anybody.

Maybe that's the most comfortable relationship adults can have.

The thing that stayed with me most, however, wasn't the scenery.

It was the people.

Years ago, riding in a taxi on the left side of the road in Sydney left me slightly traumatized.

This time I decided to tempt fate again.

I rented a right-hand-drive car.

My first few hours behind the wheel were...

Conservative.

Actually, "terrified" is probably a more accurate word.

Cars kept passing me on the right.

I had already prepared myself for what I considered the universal language of impatient drivers:

Being judged.

Or perhaps receiving the famous American middle finger.

Instead...

Every car that passed gave me a little wave.

Or a polite nod.

As if to say,

"Excuse me, I'll just go ahead."

My only thought was:

"Wait... I'm the slow one. Why are you apologizing to me?"

Later, I drove through several construction zones.

Workers stood by the roadside holding soft fabric warning signs.

Open.

Close.

Open.

Close.

Like a giant hand-operated GIF.

No electricity.

No AI.

Surprisingly smooth frame rate.

Every single time a car passed, they bowed.

As if saying,

"Sorry for taking a few seconds of your time."

I couldn't help wondering how many hundreds of bows their backs endured every day.

Then I thought about road construction in the United States.

Close one lane.

Forty-minute traffic jam.

No explanation.

No apology.

Six or seven workers watching one person work.

And another standing perfectly still with a stop sign.

Meanwhile, your navigation app calmly announces:

"Estimated delay: 38 minutes."

As though those 38 minutes had never belonged to you in the first place.

One morning at breakfast, I noticed an elderly gentleman wiping tables.

Spray bottle in his left hand.

His right hand held out in front of the nozzle.

Not for himself.

For the people waiting nearby.

He didn't want the mist to splash onto them.

I watched him for several minutes.

It suddenly occurred to me that even a spray bottle could have good manners.

Later, in Furano, I stopped to buy one of the region's famous melons.

I couldn't read the Japanese labels.

So I picked the one that simply looked nicest to me.

At the register, the shopkeeper gently stopped me.

She gestured for quite a while.

For a split second I panicked.

"Oh no... Did I accidentally pick the store's priceless display melon?"

I opened Google Translate.

Her message appeared:

"This one won't be ripe for another three days. I thought you probably wanted to eat one today."

I nodded so enthusiastically I nearly gave myself whiplash.

She walked me to another shelf.

Picked up a much prettier melon.

"This one," she smiled.

"Today."

I rushed back to my hotel.

The very first thing I did was cut it open.

Not because I was hungry.

Well... not entirely.

I was simply curious.

She was right.

It was perfect.

Soft enough to melt in your mouth.

Sweet enough to feel like cheating.

That was the day I learned melons apparently come with appointment schedules.

Accurate to the day.

Later, I stopped by Rokkatei to buy some desserts.

As the cashier packed everything, she carefully checked the expiration date on every single item.

Then she pointed to the matcha daifuku.

"Please eat this by tomorrow."

For a moment, I felt she understood my eating schedule over the next twenty-four hours better than my own mother.

On the last day, I stopped for gas.

I stood in front of a pump covered entirely in Japanese, studying the buttons without making much progress.

Before I knew it, the station attendant came sprinting out of the office.

Not walking.

Actually running.

The urgency suggested that if he arrived one second later, I might accidentally blow up the entire gas station.

After filling the tank, he apologized repeatedly in hesitant English for making me wait.

I was the one who felt embarrassed.

Looking back, nothing dramatic happened during the trip.

There were no movie moments.

No earth-shattering revelations.

And certainly no grand conclusion about "what Japanese people are like."

Just countless ordinary people...

Who chose to do one little thing more.

One extra reminder.

A few extra steps.

One hand shielding a stranger from a spray bottle.

One more bow.

At the time, each gesture felt so small that I assumed I'd forget it within five minutes.

Yet after the trip ended...

Those were the only things I remembered.

Eventually I realized that's what makes travel so fascinating.

It's rarely about what you see.

It's about what quietly changes in you after you come home.

Maybe the next time I catch up to someone driving well below the speed limit...

I won't honk.

Maybe I'll simply wave.

And let them know—

It's okay.

Sometimes...

Going a little slower isn't such a bad way to travel.

title: F. William Sunderman — The Invisible Threads of a Life
summary: From Tuberculosis Research to eCommerce: How Unexpected Encounters Reveal the Threads That Connect a Life It's graduation season, and an email from the University of Toronto alumni office unexpectedly landed in my...
body:
From Tuberculosis Research to eCommerce: How Unexpected Encounters Reveal the Threads That Connect a Life

It's graduation season, and an email from the University of Toronto alumni office unexpectedly landed in my inbox, inviting me back to campus to celebrate a new graduating class. Like most alumni messages, it was meant to look forward. Instead, it quietly carried me backward—to my own graduate years, when I spent my days studying tuberculosis and was convinced my future would remain in molecular biology and microbiology.

Life, of course, had other plans.

Over the years, I've wandered through sales, stem cell research, real estate, insurance, cooking, archery, skiing, scuba diving, and eventually eCommerce.

Looking back, I sometimes wonder how so many seemingly unrelated chapters could possibly belong to the same life.

Perhaps it was nostalgia.

This afternoon, while browsing Kyobo Book Centre in Gangnam, a book on the history of laboratory medicine caught my eye. As I flipped through the pages, one name immediately stood out:

F. William Sunderman.

Most people remember him as the physician-scientist who pioneered proficiency testing and helped establish many of the quality standards that modern laboratory medicine relies upon today.

What fascinated me even more was that he was also an accomplished violinist.

Having survived tuberculosis himself, he continued practicing music every day while pursuing science with equal discipline, remaining intellectually active and performing well beyond his hundredth birthday.

His life wasn't a straight line.

It was a tapestry woven from science, music, discipline, curiosity, and resilience.

The more I read, the more I understood why his story resonated with me.

The precision he pursued in laboratory medicine reminds me of the standards I strive for in business.

His love of music echoes the joy I find in wine tasting, cooking, and sports.

His encounter with tuberculosis takes me back to my own years at the lab bench.

And his willingness to cross disciplines, again and again throughout his life, feels strangely familiar as I continue navigating between science, business, and creativity.

Over time, I've come to believe that life is rarely linear.

What look like detours are often tributaries flowing toward the same sea.

Curiosity changes its subject.

Precision changes its application.

Resilience changes its battlefield.

But their essence remains the same.

Perhaps passion never truly disappears.

It simply finds new ways to express itself.

And perhaps reinvention isn't about becoming someone new.

It's about becoming more completely yourself.

Sometimes the most meaningful encounters arrive quietly—

an unexpected email from your alma mater,

an unplanned afternoon in a bookstore,

and the discovery of someone else's life that somehow helps you understand your own.

title: The Cicadas Still Sing Every Summer, but They're Never the Same Voices
summary: On my way downstairs to the gym today, I came across two cicadas. The first was green, lying motionless on the concrete. I picked it up and placed it on a nearby tree.
body:
On my way downstairs to the gym today, I came across two cicadas.

The first was green, lying motionless on the concrete.

I picked it up and placed it on a nearby tree.

Almost immediately, it inserted its mouthparts into the bark and began feeding on the sap.

It wasn't dead.

Just exhausted.

A few steps later, I found another one.

It had just emerged from its shell, but the transformation hadn't gone well.

One wing was still stuck to the old exoskeleton, crumpled tightly together no matter how hard it struggled.

I carefully separated the wing from the shell, trying not to damage it, then found a little water, hoping the wing might still unfold.

It was already too late.

I tried placing it on several different trees.

Each time, it managed to climb only a few inches before slipping back to the ground and ending up on its back, exhausted.

I didn't leave.

I sat beside it, waited for it to recover, then gently placed it back on the trunk.

It fell.

I lifted it back up.

It fell again.

So I lifted it again.

I don't know how long we repeated this.

Eventually, it found its grip.

It didn't rush upward.

It simply climbed—

one tiny step at a time.

At that moment, a line from Jurassic Park suddenly came back to me:

Life finds a way.

Later, I looked up the life cycle of a cicada.

They spend three to five years underground.

The part of life they spend in sunlight lasts only a single summer.

Medical training teaches us to think about life through the lens of species.

A failed emergence means no reproduction.

From the perspective of natural selection, this cicada would likely never pass on its genes.

But sitting beneath that tree, watching it struggle upward, I realized that a species and an individual are two very different ways of looking at life.

Natural selection cares about continuation.

Life itself may care only about having been lived.

Even if this cicada never leaves behind its DNA,

it still climbed out of the darkness.

It still held onto a tree.

It still felt the summer wind.

And it still heard the song that belonged to its own brief season.

I eventually continued on to the gym.

Before I left, I looked back one last time.

It was still climbing.

Slowly.

But climbing.

title: The Two Things St. Louis Left Me With
summary: One was the weather. The other was its people. Summers regularly climbed past 40°C, wrapped in thick Midwestern humidity that made breathing feel like work.
body:
One was the weather.

The other was its people.

Summers regularly climbed past 40°C, wrapped in thick Midwestern humidity that made breathing feel like work.

Spring brought tornado sirens so often they almost became background noise.

When the alarms sounded, everyone headed for the basement.

Cars on rooftops.

Baseball-sized hail.

It was simply part of life.

The other thing I remember is the people.

During the years I worked there, I met an extraordinary number of people who were genuinely kind, humble, and uncomplicated.

I've lived and worked in many places since then, but nowhere else has that kind of sincerity felt quite so common.

Today I received an email celebrating the 25th anniversary of Give Kids A Smile, and immediately thought of someone I haven't seen in years:

Dr. Jeff Dalin.

More than a decade ago, while working at Sigma-Aldrich, I was preparing my dental school applications in my spare time.

On weekends, I volunteered with Give Kids A Smile, providing free dental screenings and cleanings for children from low-income families.

Back then, the organization was remarkably small.

It was essentially Jeff—and a handful of volunteers like us.

Working together weekend after weekend, we gradually became friends despite the difference in our ages.

Later, after moving back to the West Coast, I spent some time helping raise funds, hoping to bring the program there.

But healthcare systems and community needs differed so much between regions that the effort never truly took off.

Time passed.

Today, seeing Give Kids A Smile celebrate its 25th anniversary, I also noticed that Jeff received the American Dental Association Humanitarian Award a few years ago.

I couldn't help smiling.

It's easy to overlook work that seems ordinary.

It's much harder to devote decades to doing that ordinary work exceptionally well.

I'm genuinely happy for all of them.

title: A Michelin-Starred Afternoon at 4:00 PM
summary: Q2 ended. I took a little over two weeks off. My first week back began with a meeting. One agenda item. Bonuses. Should we pay them? Or not? I've always thought it was a pretty simple question.
body:
Q2 ended.

I took a little over two weeks off.

My first week back began with a meeting.

One agenda item.

Bonuses.

Should we pay them?

Or not?

I've always thought it was a pretty simple question.

People did the work.

Pay them.

Meeting over.

Instead, a room full of people spent two hours discussing it.

Then someone actually turned to me and asked,

"So... what would you think if your team didn't receive bonuses?"

What would I think?

I'd probably have to cover my eyes to answer.

Not being able to protect your team feels a bit like a parent who can't protect their own children.

It hurts.

What hurt even more was realizing this was still somehow up for debate.

I sat there looking thoughtful.

I probably looked asleep.

Around me, mouths kept moving.

PowerPoint slides kept changing.

Arguments kept multiplying.

Somewhere in the middle of it all, I felt a yawn coming.

Yawning in front of fifteen people isn't exactly polite.

So I held it in.

The yawn never came.

Instead...

...it became a burp.

The burp charged halfway up my throat.
