I swallowed it back down.

That single heroic swallow somehow squeezed two tears out of my eyes.

Just as I reached up to wipe them away naturally, the person beside me—who was passionately making another point—looked over.

I'll never forget that expression.

It seemed to say,

"Wow... is this discussion really that emotional?"

Or maybe,

"If something's making you this miserable, you should share it with the group."

Two hours later, the meeting ended exactly where it had started.

No decision.

Only my battery had died.

I opened Outlook.

Maybe the day could get worse.

Instead, I discovered tomorrow was a public holiday.

I have no idea what holiday Korea was celebrating.

Didn't matter.

Any holiday is a good holiday.

I immediately canceled my afternoon meetings.

Today, I officially stopped being a responsible adult.

It was time to forage for food like a wild animal.

I've always believed emotional eating serves an important purpose.

At the very least, it rents happiness for about thirty minutes.

So I wandered into Insadong.

It's the sort of neighborhood that sells absolutely everything.

Calligraphy.

Dragon's beard candy.

Comics.

Handmade stamps.

Souvenirs.

And countless things I couldn't identify but somehow still wanted to buy.

It's close to Gyeongbokgung Palace and packed with tourists.

Imagine Beijing's Wangfujing...

scaled down to Korean proportions.

As I turned into a narrow alley, I noticed a line.

Years of living in Asia have taught me one simple rule:

The longer the line,

the better the food.

I hesitated for exactly one second.

Join first?

Or investigate first?

Curiosity won.

I walked to the front and peeked inside.

Dumplings?

People were lining up... for dumplings?

Then my eyes drifted to the sign beside the door.

Michelin.

Several consecutive years.

My pupils immediately expanded about six times.

Suddenly I wasn't tired anymore.

The morning meeting didn't even seem that terrible.

Maybe life was fair after all.

Take away my team's bonuses...

Give me a Michelin restaurant.

I happily joined the queue.

The line in front of me became shorter and shorter.

The line behind me...

never appeared.

Not one person.

I felt oddly proud.

Apparently not everyone possessed my level of strategic thinking.

Finally it was my turn.

I lifted one foot across the doorway.

A middle-aged woman instantly crossed her arms.

❌

Then she launched into rapid-fire Korean.

"...aniyo... imnida..."

I froze.

Looked down at myself.

Crocs.

Sure, maybe a little casual.

Wait...

Was there actually a dress code for dumplings?

After living in Korea for a year and a half, my Korean was still only slightly better than that of an unusually intelligent stray dog.

Seeing my blank stare, she pointed toward the business hours posted beside the entrance.

Closed from 2:00 to 4:00 PM.

I looked at my watch.

2:00.

Well...

1:60.

Then she said something else.

Only then did I realize the problem wasn't that I was late.

It was that my foot was physically preventing her from closing the door.

I quietly pulled my foot back.

The door shut instantly.

Click.

With the precision of a NASA rocket launch.

Suddenly I understood why nobody had been standing behind me.

I looked again.

Reopens at 4:00 PM.

Two hours.

Two whole hours.

Time is valuable.

Surely nobody would wait two hours just for dumplings.

I stood there.

Thought about it for three seconds.

Then, entirely predictably...

I decided to wait.

Look on the bright side.

Two hours from now...

I'd be today's first customer.

Victory.

Standing outside for two hours, however, looked suspiciously like begging.

Squatting looked even worse.

So I wandered around.

I told myself dinner always tastes better than lunch.

Repeated it enough times.

Eventually I believed it.

It was scorching hot.

Should I grab a snack?

No.

That would be disrespectful to my 4:00 PM Michelin experience.

Water was acceptable.

I bought one bottle.

Gone in seconds.

Still hot.

Nearby, I spotted a tiny art gallery.

More importantly...

it had air conditioning.

I entered immediately.

Not for the art.

For the climate.

To justify staying, I examined every painting with extraordinary seriousness.

Long enough that anyone watching would've assumed I was an art collector.

In reality...

I was simply maximizing my air-conditioning efficiency.

After a while I got thirsty again.

Bought another bottle of water.

Returned.

Studied the next painting.

At some point I realized I wasn't appreciating art anymore.

I was intermittently irrigating the gallery.

The owner had begun watching me with increasing suspicion.

I imagined his internal monologue.

"This foreigner seems fascinated by my paintings..."

"So why does he keep leaving every ten minutes?"

Eventually he approached and launched into an enthusiastic explanation—in Korean.

Perhaps about the paintings.

Perhaps about the artist.

Perhaps about the prices.

I understood exactly none of it.

So I smiled.

And nodded.

When you don't speak the language,

nodding is humanity's safest universal response.

To avoid further conversation, I slowly drifted toward the back corner.

Not because the painting there was exceptional.

Because that corner had the strongest air conditioning...

and the owner couldn't see me.

By then I was genuinely hungry.

Time crawled.

Finally.

3:50 PM.

I bowed apologetically to the gallery owner.

I'd spent nearly two hours with his artwork...

and bought absolutely nothing.

I felt like an art thief.

Then I sprinted toward the restaurant.

The alley was quiet.

I arrived first.

Within minutes, people began materializing behind me.

One.

Two.

Five.

Ten.

As if they'd been summoned by invisible magnets.

Did everyone know the restaurant reopened exactly at four?

3:55.

Then another crisis struck.

Those two bottles of water suddenly demanded immediate attention.

If I went to the restroom now...

I'd lose first place.

If I didn't...

I risked becoming Insadong's most unforgettable tourist.

For the first time in my life, I seriously weighed the relative importance of my stomach versus my bladder.

Thankfully...

the door opened.

The same woman recognized me instantly.

She paused.

Her expression practically shouted,

"You actually waited two hours?"

Then she smiled.

And waved me inside.

That wasn't just a wave.

It was the gates of heaven opening.

I shot through them so quickly that even she looked surprised.

Unfortunately, my first destination wasn't my table.

It was what I believed to be the restroom.

I pushed open the door.

Not the restroom.

The kitchen.

Two chefs froze.

I froze.

Three seconds later the entire kitchen shouted in perfect harmony:

"OUT!"

I backed out while bowing repeatedly.

At that moment I think every Korean word I'd ever learned left my mouth simultaneously.

Eventually I found the actual restroom.

Half my body weight disappeared immediately.

Now...

I was finally ready for Michelin dumplings.

The restaurant had only seven or eight tables.

Within minutes every seat was full.

The menu was refreshingly simple.

Pork dumplings.

Kimchi dumplings.

Mushroom dumplings.

Then...

larger portions of pork.

Larger portions of kimchi.

Larger portions of mushroom.

It reminded me of my dad's cooking.

His four signature dishes were:

Tomatoes with eggs.

Eggs with tomatoes.

Tomatoes and eggs together.

Eggs and tomatoes together.

Since I was already here...

I decided to experience everything.

The waiter stood patiently beside me.

I pointed from the top of the menu...

all the way to the bottom.

He waited for my finger to stop.

It didn't.

Instead, I started over.

Each item I pointed at...

I held up one finger.

"One."

Human fingers truly are one of civilization's greatest inventions.

They indicate both direction and quantity.

Especially useful when you're functionally illiterate.

The waiter looked uncertain.

Then circled the menu with his pen.

Everything?

"Ne!"

I answered with the loudest Korean word I knew.

Still unconvinced, he confirmed again.

I spread both arms wide and drew an enormous circle in the air.

Everything.

Every single one.

Don't leave anything out.

Finally he nodded and disappeared into the kitchen.

Though not before turning around one last time to look at me.

I imagine he was wondering,

"Exactly how long has this foreigner been starving?"

Soon steel bowls and little side dishes filled the table.

Kimchi.

Soup.

Various mysterious liquids.

Korean meals sometimes resemble chemistry labs.

All the reagents arrive first.

The main experiment comes later.

Then...

the dumplings arrived.

I stared.

What...

...was this?

Standing proudly on the plate...

were objects approximately the size of my fist.

Technically, yes.

They were dumplings.

They had wrappers.

They had filling.

They were neatly sealed.

But these belonged to an entirely different species from the dumplings I knew.

An ostrich is a bird.

A hummingbird is also a bird.

That doesn't mean they belong at the same dinner table.

Before I'd recovered,

the second plate arrived.

Then the third.

Three mountains of dumplings occupied my entire table like a gathering of sumo wrestlers.

I looked at the waiter.

My expression clearly asked,

"You call these dumplings?"

He smiled.

Then slowly reenacted my earlier gesture.

Drawing one enormous circle in the air.

Everything.

Right?

Only then did I realize.

He hadn't misunderstood me.

He had understood me perfectly.

Nearby diners began glancing over.

Then at my table.

Then back at me.

Some looked impressed.

Some looked concerned.

Perhaps wondering whether a homeless shelter existed somewhere inside my stomach.

I remained silent.

For about two seconds.

Then remembered my younger days leaving all-you-can-eat buffets supported only by sheer determination and nearby walls.

If I'd survived that...

I could survive Michelin dumplings.

I picked one up.

Heavy.

Remarkably heavy.

It felt less like food...

more like lifting gym equipment with chopsticks.

I bit into it.

Paused.

No flavor.

Not bad.

Not good.

Simply...

nothing.

Like someone had carefully wrapped air inside dough.

To verify my taste buds still worked,

I took another bite.

Now my mouth was so full I resembled a squirrel storing peanuts for winter.

I grabbed water.

Swallowed.

Thought carefully.

What exactly had I just tasted?

Nothing.

Surely...

this couldn't be Michelin?

I tried the kimchi dumpling.

Nothing.

Mushroom.

Nothing.

Pork.

Still nothing.

Three fillings.

One identical absence of flavor.

That, in its own way, was impressive.

Ordinary restaurants make different fillings taste different.

Michelin had somehow made them all taste exactly the same.

Which is to say...

they tasted like almost nothing.

After sampling two bites from each variety, I was already full.

Around me, everyone else ate calmly.

Nobody looked delighted.

Nobody looked disappointed.

Nobody stared at dumplings questioning the meaning of life.

Then I noticed something else.

An entire family's order occupied less table space than mine.

Finally I understood.

The waiter hadn't been doubting me.

He'd been trying to save me.

And I'd enthusiastically rejected every attempt.

What now?

I searched desperately for explanations.

Maybe they were organic.

Maybe healthy.

Maybe Koreans believed salt caused hypertension.

Or perhaps Michelin had simply evolved beyond seasoning.

The dumplings sat there quietly.

Like victorious terracotta warriors.

Eventually...

my stomach surrendered first.

I waved over the waiter.

Pointed at the mountain of dumplings.

Then toward the door.

Then mimed putting everything into a bag.

I don't know the Korean word for "takeout."

Fortunately every waiter on Earth speaks interpretive mime.

He nodded.

For the first time all day, he looked completely relaxed.

As if thinking,

"I knew we'd end up here."

A few minutes later I walked out carrying an enormous bag.

It was astonishingly heavy.

Less like leftover dinner...

more like leaving the gym with a dumbbell.

Walking home, I realized the entire day had unfolded differently from what I'd expected.

I expected my team to receive bonuses.

They didn't.

I expected an afternoon surprise.

Instead I found a locked door.

I expected two hours of waiting to end with unforgettable Michelin food.

Instead I received giant flavorless dumplings.

Life has a peculiar sense of humor.

Just when you think it's about to turn left...

it turns right.

Then takes another unexpected turn.

Back home, I stared at the bag of dumplings.

A Warren Buffett quote came to mind:

The secret to happiness is having fewer expectations.

Today...

that sounded especially wise.

I quietly carried the Michelin dumplings downstairs.

Tapped my card.

Opened the food-waste bin.

Dropped them in.

Beep.

Payment successful.

I stood there silently for two seconds.

One final surprise.

Apparently...

throwing away bad Michelin food costs extra.

title: The Coolest Buddha I've Ever Met
summary: A friend flew in to visit from Xicun this weekend, so we wandered around Seoul with no real plan. Somehow, we ended up at what looked like a very serious International Buddhism Expo.
body:
A friend flew in to visit from Xicun this weekend, so we wandered around Seoul with no real plan.

Somehow, we ended up at what looked like a very serious International Buddhism Expo.

My expectations were simple:

Incense.

Prayer beads.

A little wisdom about inner peace.

Instead...

there was a line stretching hundreds of meters.

And most of the people waiting?

Young Koreans.

We looked at each other.

"Something isn't adding up."

The moment we walked inside, I realized my imagination had been far too limited.

Apparently...

Buddha can wear a tailored suit.

(And somehow pull it off.)

Monks can dance.

(Not quite K-pop idols... but honestly, just as entertaining.)

And someone was selling "INNER PEACE" T-shirts for ₩8,000.

I almost bought one.

For a brief moment I wondered if I'd accidentally walked into a Buddha-themed pop-up festival instead of a religious exhibition.

One thing became clear.

Korean exhibitions never follow the script.

But somehow...

they almost never miss aesthetically.

The entire place felt joyful.

Not forced happiness.

The kind that naturally shows up on people's faces.

It made me realize something.

Maybe spiritual practice isn't about escaping the world.

Maybe it's about learning how to enjoy living in it a little more.

K-pop competes on the stage.

B-pop competes for inner peace.

title: My First K-pop Concert
summary: Part curiosity. Part feeling that living in Korea without experiencing K-pop somehow left my Seoul story unfinished. So I went to Gyeongbokgung Palace to catch BTS's homecoming event.
body:
Part curiosity.

Part feeling that living in Korea without experiencing K-pop somehow left my Seoul story unfinished.

So I went to Gyeongbokgung Palace to catch BTS's homecoming event.

The media estimated around 300,000 people, with overseas visitors more than doubling.

Numbers like that have a strange gravity.

It's hard not to be pulled in.

The concert started at 8 p.m.

I arrived shortly after four.

Following the crowds through security, I made my way toward Gwanghwamun.

The place was already packed.

Everyone seemed to be holding reservation tickets.

Only then did I realize...

you actually needed reservations.

Well.

Too late now.

Rather than fight for the perfect view, I did what was either smart—or just lazy.

I found a café overlooking the venue, ordered a matcha latte, and watched everything through the window.

Turns out that was the real VIP seat.

No pushing.

No heat.

No noise.

Just air conditioning and a front-row view as the crowd slowly grew larger.

Around eight, I finished my drink and headed downstairs.

The lights came on.

The music started.

The cheers erupted exactly on cue.

There were people from everywhere—different languages, different faces—all mixed into one enormous crowd.

After listening for a while, one completely inappropriate thought popped into my head.

...That's it?

This is one of the biggest groups in the world?

Maybe my expectations were too high.

Or maybe I'd misunderstood K-pop altogether.

So instead of judging the performance, I started watching the audience.

Some people were ecstatic.

Others looked surprisingly calm.

A bit like me.

Since I'd already committed the afternoon—and now the evening—I figured I might as well stay until the end.

Maybe one song would finally click.

It never did.

By the time it was over, my legs were numb.

My only real feeling was mild regret.

I'd just invested an entire afternoon because of a reputation.

On stage were performers who simply didn't match my own image of masculinity.

The music, choreography, and style weren't things I naturally connected with.

They performed with incredible energy.

I could see the effort.

It just wasn't for me.

Walking home, I remembered a book I'd been listening to earlier that day:

The Social Animal.

It argues two things.

First, humans naturally follow crowds.

Second, our taste and judgment are deeply shaped by past experience.

That afternoon proved both points perfectly.

Why had I come?

Because words like "300,000 people" and "global superstars" are powerful social signals.

They create a gentle kind of peer pressure.

Why didn't I enjoy it?

Because I've spent years listening to jazz, blues, country, rock, French music, Disney soundtracks, and powerful vocalists.

Even my idea of what feels masculine has been shaped by a lifetime of different cultural references.

I wasn't simply listening to music.

I was measuring one culture using another culture's ruler.

No wonder it didn't resonate.

The problem wasn't the concert.

And it wasn't really me, either.

It was simply...

perception.

Maybe the more honest conclusion is this:

Everything simply is.

Things aren't inherently good or bad.

They look different depending on where you're standing.

Looking back, the value of that afternoon wasn't checking "Attend a K-pop concert" off my bucket list.

It was realizing something much more interesting.

I like to think I'm an independent thinker.

Someone who forms opinions rationally.

But underneath all that...

I'm still just another social animal.

So perhaps next time I feel absolutely certain about something, I'll pause for a moment and ask myself:

Is this really a fact?

Or is it simply the perspective I've grown accustomed to?

Experience Doesn't Always Make Us Wiser—Sometimes It Just Reinforces Our Biases

title: Thoughts after reading Third Millennium Thinking
summary: Every flight between the U.S. and Korea leaves me feeling as if different parts of me are traveling at different speeds. My body is still somewhere in the comfort of home in Seattle.
body:
Every flight between the U.S. and Korea leaves me feeling as if different parts of me are traveling at different speeds.

My body is still somewhere in the comfort of home in Seattle.

My thoughts are drifting quietly above the Pacific.

Meanwhile, my subconscious has already landed, preparing itself for another round of Korean conversations.

Maybe that's my own definition of distance.

From space, there are no countries or continents—just one small blue planet, and an even smaller version of ourselves living on it.

During the flight I finished Third Millennium Thinking, written by an extraordinary trio: Nobel Prize-winning physicist Saul Perlmutter, philosopher John Campbell, and psychologist Robert MacCoun.

Since 2011, they've taught an interdisciplinary course at UC Berkeley with a deceptively simple goal: helping people learn how to think, not what to think.

The course teaches students how to separate facts from opinions, ask better questions before rushing to conclusions, think in probabilities rather than certainties, and work with people who see the world differently instead of staying inside comfortable echo chambers.

It's a framework that feels especially relevant today, when information is abundant but clarity isn't.

One story from the book really stayed with me.

While working as a postdoc, Saul Perlmutter's research team had the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to observe Supernova 1987A. Their telescope detected what appeared to be a pulsing neutron star. After correcting the data for Doppler effects, an almost perfectly smooth sine wave emerged.

It looked like evidence of a planet orbiting the neutron star.

The discovery was exciting enough to be published in Nature.

A career-defining moment.

Then they went back to observe it again.

This time the signal appeared... then disappeared... then reappeared.

Eventually they discovered the truth.

Their telescope had been so sensitive that it was picking up tiny electronic interference from equipment on a neighboring mountain. Ironically, the data corrections had transformed random noise into what looked like a beautiful scientific discovery.

There had never been a planet.

The paper had to be withdrawn.

That story perfectly captures what science really is.

It's not about always being right.

It's about noticing patterns, testing them, getting things wrong, correcting yourself, and slowly moving closer to the truth.

A few ideas from the book have stayed with me ever since.

Sometimes I think I'm reasoning, when I'm really just telling myself a story I already wanted to believe.

The experts I trust most aren't the ones who never make mistakes. They're the ones willing to admit uncertainty and change their minds.

Instead of asking whether something is absolutely true or false, ask how confident you should be.

Disagreement isn't the enemy. It's often where better ideas begin.

Knowing what you don't know is far more valuable than being confidently wrong. Skepticism isn't pessimism—it's the courage to admit that reality may be more complicated than we'd like.

Since finishing the book, I've been trying to ask myself four questions more often:

Is this actually a fact, or just the story I'd like to believe?

When everyone agrees, do I still have the courage to ask, "Are we sure?"

When I see a perfect pattern, have I considered the possibility that it's just noise?

Instead of saying I'm certain, can I honestly describe my confidence as a probability?

Perhaps experience doesn't automatically make us wiser.

If we're not careful, it simply makes us more confident in yesterday's assumptions.

Real thinking begins when we're willing to question ourselves.

title: Soorarai Pottru — The Dream That Shouldn't Have Worked
summary: I never paid much attention to Indian films. Then I watched Soorarai Pottru, released by Amazon Prime Video in 2020. It completely changed my mind. The movie is based on the life of G. R. Gopinath, founder of India's...
body:
I never paid much attention to Indian films.

Then I watched Soorarai Pottru, released by Amazon Prime Video in 2020.

It completely changed my mind.

The movie is based on the life of G. R. Gopinath, founder of India's first low-cost airline, and his memoir Simply Fly: A Deccan Odyssey.

At the center of the story is a heartbreaking moment.

After years of conflict with his father, the main character finally decides to go home.

But when he reaches the airport, economy tickets are sold out.

He begs.

He pleads.

Security drags him away.

He spends the rest of the journey desperately piecing together buses, trucks, and whatever transportation he can find.

By the time he arrives...

his father has already been cremated.

In his final moments, his father imagines seeing his son return in military uniform.

But it's only a vision.

Reality comes too late.

What makes the scene so powerful is that it isn't exaggerated.

It reflects a painful reality for millions of people.

For those without money, even something as simple as arriving in time can become an impossible luxury.

That loss becomes the reason he decides to pursue what everyone else believes is an impossible dream:

Making air travel affordable for ordinary people.

Everything that follows feels almost suffocating.

Powerful competitors try to crush him.

Regulations work against him.

Banks trap him.

Bureaucracy slows everything down.

Every time he's knocked down, he somehow finds a way to stand back up.

But what moved me most wasn't his determination.

It was the people around him.

His mother quietly gives him her life savings.

His wife keeps the family afloat by baking bread while refusing to let him give up.

His friends carry him when he has nothing left.

Even an officer who once looked down on him eventually chooses to stand beside him.

The world can be incredibly cruel.

But kindness never disappears.

Sometimes it's those small acts of kindness that carry someone through impossible moments.

When the first plane finally takes off...

it doesn't feel like victory.

It feels like a quiet answer to a question the world had ignored for too long.

What stayed with me wasn't just the story.

It was this:

We aren't defined by how many times we fall.

We're defined by the one more time we choose to get back up.

Fear never really disappears.

We simply grow bigger than it.

Nothing we go through is wasted.

Every failure quietly prepares us for what's next.

And when ordinary people refuse to quit...

they slowly make the world a little fairer.

If you're struggling, doubting yourself, or wondering whether to keep going—

there's almost always one more step waiting.

Take it.

title: A Small Alley
summary: A year ago, I never would have imagined that one day I'd be wandering alone through a quiet alley in Gangnam, Seoul... trying to clear my head after realizing my team needed to recruit forty thousand marketplace...
body:
A year ago, I never would have imagined that one day I'd be wandering alone through a quiet alley in Gangnam, Seoul...

trying to clear my head after realizing my team needed to recruit forty thousand marketplace sellers in just four weeks.

Life has a strange sense of humor.

I also never expected a Monday night to feel so beautiful.

There were persimmons hanging from roadside trees, almost ready to ripen.

Tiny izakayas glowing beneath red lanterns.

A New York-style bagel bakery.

An Irish pub already decorated for Christmas.

A Thai restaurant.

Street food stalls.

And dozens of quirky little restaurants that somehow all looked inviting.

It felt as though the alley itself was telling me,

"Stop overthinking."

"Eat something first."

Maybe some answers aren't found by thinking.

Maybe they're found by walking.

By catching the smell of food drifting out of a restaurant.

Or simply by noticing a cluster of ripe persimmons overhead.

Whenever you're feeling overwhelmed, go for a walk.

And when life is going well...

go anyway.

If you keep walking long enough, you'll discover that life is a lot like a small alley.

The destination matters less than you think.

The best moments are usually hidden in the few unplanned steps you almost didn't take.

Maybe that's what being truly relaxed feels like.

On an ordinary Monday evening...

not rushing anywhere,

not chasing anyone,

not even watching the time—

just following wherever your mood takes you.

Sometimes that's enough to stumble upon an entire street full of quiet magic.

Take your time.

You'll figure it out.

There are almost always more solutions than problems.

title: Seoul After Dark: The Night a Poster Changed My Plans
summary: After spending the entire day reading, my brain had officially gone on strike. So that evening I wandered over to a nearby church to listen to some music, made a small donation, and headed home.
body:
After spending the entire day reading, my brain had officially gone on strike.

So that evening I wandered over to a nearby church to listen to some music, made a small donation, and headed home.

The night breeze was perfect.

I was strolling along without any destination when a giant bright-red poster suddenly stopped me in my tracks.

BEST MUSICAL.

The color. The typography. The drama.

It screamed Broadway.

Curiosity has always been my biggest weakness, so I walked over for a closer look.

Moulin Rouge.

And not just any production—the brand-new Seoul run.

The poster said Blue Square.

I remember thinking, Where's that?

I kept walking.

Then something almost too convenient happened.

I looked up.

The building right in front of me had enormous neon letters glowing across the top:

BLUE SQUARE.

I actually laughed out loud.

The universe wasn't exactly being subtle.

Mission Impossible began:

Find a ticket.

I walked inside.

The lobby was packed.

People were crowding around ticket machines, printing reservations before the show started.

I thought, Someone who just wandered in off the street has absolutely no chance.

But my feet kept carrying me toward the box office anyway.

The line looked hopeless.

Then the optimist in me suggested,

"Why not check online first?"

So I pulled out my phone—which was already running low on battery—and opened the ticket website.

Instantly...

Korean.

Nothing but Korean.

Not one recognizable word.

I kept tapping and scrolling.

The more I scrolled, the more confused I became.

Is this the login button?

Or logout?

Or... buy one get one free?

Honestly, I had no idea what I was pressing.

After a few frantic rounds with Google Translate, a form suddenly appeared.

"Great," I thought.

"Finally—the checkout page."

No.

It said:

Please create an account.

Fine.

I filled everything in.

Then came the next message.

Please verify your Korean phone number.

My soul briefly left my body.

"I only found out where Blue Square is thirty seconds ago... and now you expect me to verify a Korean phone number?"

Meanwhile I was standing in the middle of the lobby holding my phone in the air like someone trying to summon better reception from heaven.

The countdown to showtime kept ticking.

The crowd grew smaller.

My heartbeat grew faster.

I was seconds away from giving up.

Then the unreasonable version of myself—the one that only shows up late at night—whispered,

"Try one more thing."

So I walked over to the only empty ticket window and handed my last bit of hope to the woman behind the counter.

She typed rapidly.

Her English carried the unmistakable melody of a Korean accent.

After a few seconds she looked up.

Her eyes lit up.

"There is..."

She paused.

"ONE ticket left!"

My pupils instantly expanded about six times.

I didn't even ask the price.

"YES!"

Credit card.

Ticket.

Sprint.

An usher waved me into the theater literally seconds before the lights dimmed.

The auditorium was stunning.

It immediately reminded me of Seattle's Paramount Theatre and Broadway houses in New York.

Everything glowed in deep crimson.

Velvet seats.

Golden balconies.

Warm theatrical lighting.

It felt less like Seoul and more like I'd somehow wandered into Paris after dark.

Then, just as I settled into my seat...

my evening became even more memorable.

I leaned forward slightly, trying to get a better look at the stage.

A theater attendant walked over.

I assumed she was welcoming guests.

Instead, with an incredibly polite smile, she quietly said,

"Please sit back. Back on the seat."

She had identified me as the foreigner within seconds.

I froze.

Really?

This is something people get corrected for?

The last time someone told me how to sit was probably first grade.

I looked around.

Everyone else was sitting perfectly upright.

Perfect posture.

Perfect stillness.

It looked less like a theater audience and more like a national sitting examination.

I almost laughed.

Normally I'm very much a rules are meant to be broken kind of person.

For about half a second I considered arguing.

Then I remembered my Korean vocabulary.

It wasn't exactly built for philosophical debates.

I had already won the lottery by getting the last ticket.

Fine.

I'd sit properly.

Then the orchestra began.

Within moments I was transported to nineteenth-century Paris.

Extravagant costumes.

Energetic can-can dancers.

And Korean performers passionately singing songs by Lady Gaga and Katy Perry.

It was wonderfully strange.

Completely familiar.

Completely new.

I didn't understand a single line of Korean dialogue.

But I already knew the story.

And emotions don't need subtitles.

When the tragedy reached its final scene, I could hear people around me quietly crying.

My own thought was much simpler.

Turns out you don't always have to fly back to New York to experience Broadway magic.

Sometimes it finds you on an ordinary street in Seoul.

The best surprises in life are rarely planned.

They don't arrive after perfect preparation.

They appear because one ordinary evening, you decide to follow a tiny spark of curiosity.

You take one unexpected turn.

One unnecessary step.

One small chance.

And somehow the universe meets you halfway.

Don't overthink tomorrow.

Don't try to predict every next move.

Just try.

Just walk in.

Sometimes that's all it takes for life to surprise you.

title: The Night Seoul Once Lost
summary: It was supposed to be an ordinary afternoon. I wandered into a small museum tucked beside the U.S. Embassy in Seoul, expecting nothing in particular. Instead, I stumbled upon the history of the night.
body:
It was supposed to be an ordinary afternoon.

I wandered into a small museum tucked beside the U.S. Embassy in Seoul, expecting nothing in particular.

Instead, I stumbled upon the history of the night.

Today, Seoul after dark feels free, vibrant—almost addictive.

What few people realize is that this city once lived under a nightly curfew for 36 years (1945–1982).

The night was once taken away.

Maybe that's why it feels so alive today.

Inside the museum, the lights were deliberately dim.

As if to remind visitors that this was the story of a night that had been confiscated.

The exhibition began in 1901, when Seoul lit electric streetlights for the very first time.

That first light wasn't merely illumination.

It marked the beginning of a new era.

But light didn't necessarily bring freedom.

Soon, history entered another chapter:

Curfew.

Orders lined the walls.

No one on the streets after a certain hour.

Movement prohibited at night.

The official reasons were always the same:

Safety. Order. Stability.

Yet standing there, another thought quietly emerged.

This wasn't only about controlling a city.

It was about controlling people.

Because night is where people become... unpredictable.

Day belongs to rules.

Night belongs to people.

And human nature has never been very good at staying locked away.

Before midnight, every evening became a race home.

People rushed for the last bus.

The streets filled with anxious crowds.

Then, after midnight,

another city quietly came alive.

Go-Go clubs would pull down their metal shutters...

and keep dancing behind closed doors.

The music stayed inside.

The rules stayed outside.

At four in the morning, when the curfew was lifted, people would step back onto the streets and gather for bowls of hangover soup,

as if completing a secret ritual of freedom.

You can control time,

but never desire.

Further inside, the exhibition suddenly softened.

One entire wall was dedicated to the emotions of the night.

Day belongs to the world.

Night belongs to yourself.

And at night,

everything we hide during the day... comes back quietly.

Then I noticed two old love letters.

Yellowed paper.

Simple handwriting.

Nothing extravagant.

Yet somehow deeply moving.

With Google Translate in hand, I read them line by line.

Letter One — Dear My Beautiful Lily

"Dear my beautiful Lily..."

"Tonight the training camp is lit only by the stars.

As always, I searched for the moon. Tonight it hangs in the sky like a small fingernail.

I looked at it for a long time before returning to my dormitory with a quiet sigh.

Sometimes distant artillery and nighttime drills make the night feel endless.

But when everything grows silent, and only the stars remain, it becomes the kind of quiet that lets you hear your own heart.

Even if only in my dreams, I want to see you.

I'm writing this letter, hoping I'll fall asleep before the ink dries.

Let's meet in our dreams.

Good night."

"Let me meet you, even if only in a dream."

Letter Two — A Night in March

"A quiet night.

A deep March night.

How have you been?

I miss you.

I sit through these long hours, listening to the lullaby inside my own heart while slowly revisiting our memories.

Lying quietly in the darkness, my eyes drift in and out of focus.

All I can see is you.

Not hearing from you leaves me worried.

I've been trying to live well.

To eat properly.

To become a better version of myself.

So that the next time we meet...

you'll be happy to see me again."

"I'm trying to become someone you'd be happy to see again."

When I finished reading, the museum suddenly became very quiet.

Neither letter ever said,

"I love you."

Yet every line leaned gently toward the other person.

Back then, nights were longer.

Slower.

So longing stretched longer too.

Maybe love felt deeper back then—

not because people loved more,

but because they had to wait longer.

When I stepped outside, Seoul's nightlife had already begun.

The streets were bright.

The restaurants were full.

Everything looked perfectly normal.

Then it struck me.

None of this was inevitable.

This freedom had once been restricted.

Endured.

Longed for.

Only after all of that did it become what it is today.

If day is about order,

night is about truth.

The world becomes orderly during the day.

People become whole at night.

Night

Lights can brighten.

Roads can widen.

But the words we truly want to say...

usually arrive only after dark.

And some feelings...

only exist after dark.

Seoul's nights are lively.

But perhaps what makes them truly beautiful

is remembering that they were once

so incredibly quiet.

title: It Turns Out, I’d Been Seeing Her Every Day
summary: Before coming to Gangneung, I had already seen her countless times—at convenience stores, in cafés, and in the change from a taxi. I just never really looked.
body:
Before coming to Gangneung, I had already seen her countless times.

At convenience stores. In cafés. In the change from a taxi.

She had always been there, quietly printed on the 50,000-won note. I just never really looked.

Then, passing Ojukheon (오죽헌) in Gangneung, I suddenly realized:

this familiar face on one of Korea’s most recognizable banknotes came from here.

Ojukheon is not grand. Dark bamboo, old wooden buildings, low eaves, tucked away in a quiet corner of Gangneung. The wind moves softly through the bamboo, and time somehow seems to pass a little more slowly here.

Two people were born in this house: Shin Saimdang (신사임당), and her son, the scholar Yulgok Yi I.

Today, one appears on the 50,000-won note, the other on the 5,000-won note.

A mother and son, separated from us by centuries, somehow reunited inside the wallets of modern Korea.

There is something wonderfully charming about that.

Shin Saimdang lived during the Joseon Dynasty. She painted, wrote poetry, and practiced calligraphy. But her subjects were rarely kings, generals, or great historical scenes.

She painted grapes, flowers, insects, and birds.

Small things from an ordinary garden.

I like that about her.

Five hundred years ago, there were no cameras. If an insect landed on a leaf, or a cluster of grapes hung beneath a vine, the only way to preserve that moment was to really look at it—and then slowly place it onto paper, stroke by stroke.

Her son later became one of the most important Confucian scholars of the Joseon era. If his name feels unfamiliar, just pull out a 5,000-won note.

The mother is on 50,000 won.

The son is on 5,000.

A five-hundred-year-old family still lives neatly together in Korean wallets today.

And the mother happens to be worth ten times the son.

History, it seems, occasionally has a sense of humor.

But Shin Saimdang is remembered for more than raising a remarkable son. At a time when it was difficult for a woman to leave behind a name of her own, her paintings, poetry, and calligraphy survived.

In 2009, Korea placed her portrait on the newly issued 50,000-won note, making her the only woman featured on Korea’s current banknotes. Her grapes and insects appear there too.

Centuries ago, a woman painted a few blades of grass, a tiny insect, a cluster of grapes.

They never disappeared.

They remained with her, carried forward into the present, passing through people’s hands every day.

I never actually went inside Ojukheon.

I only passed by.

Strangely, that made me think about it even more.

Travel can be like that.

Some places you carefully explore and quickly forget. Others you never even enter, yet somehow they illuminate something familiar in an entirely new way.

She, too, once saw spring in Gangneung.

She saw the flowers in the courtyard.

Perhaps she once sat quietly in one of those rooms, bent over a page, painting a tiny insect.

Centuries passed.

The house remained.

The paintings remained.

And eventually, a country chose to place a woman who loved painting flowers, birds, grapes, and insects on its highest-denomination banknote.

Not a king.

Not a powerful official.

I like the warmth in that choice.

Now, whenever a 50,000-won note finds its way into my hand, I think I’ll look at it a little longer.

It is still the same banknote.

Only this time, I finally see her.
